## Today's Agenda

## What Tonight Covers

- Tonight is about what you are looking for, before you go looking for it
- First half: what makes an article worth keeping, and what to pull out of one when you read it, including a number you will need long before you expect to
- Second half: theory, which decides what you look at and what you ignore
- You do not need a stack of articles yet. You need to know what you are reading for, because three annotated manuscripts are due Monday, September 28

## This Is a Heavy Evening

- Tonight covers two chapters, a statistics primer, and a catalogue of theories
- The middle section involves effect sizes, and it will feel like a math class for about fifteen minutes
- You are not being asked to derive anything. You are being asked to find a number in somebody else's paper and write it down
- If the theory half feels abstract, the last slides read four real chat messages through two lenses

## Decide the List Before the Pile Exists

- Reading for annotation is a different act from reading for interest
- You extract a fixed set of things from every manuscript
- Extracting the same things every time is what makes the sources comparable to each other
- So the list comes first. Downloading twenty PDFs and deciding later what mattered gives you twenty documents you have to open twice

## What a Weak Review Sounds Like

> Hamilton, Garretson, and Kerne (2014) studied Twitch as a participatory community.
> Sjöblom and Hamari (2017) examined viewer motivations. Hilvert-Bruce and colleagues
> (2018) studied social motivations for engagement.

- These are three disconnected summaries, with nothing about how they relate
- Every sentence is driven by **who wrote the study** instead of by what is known
- This is what annotation without synthesis produces
- Most first drafts look exactly like it. It is a stage, not a verdict

## Where the Citation Goes

- By default, make the **claim** the subject and put the citation at the **end** in parentheses, as (Sjöblom & Hamari, 2017)
- Lead with the name only when that study is the point: a landmark, a definition you are adopting, or a finding you are about to argue with
- An author-led sentence announces a **study**, and a claim-led sentence states a **finding**
- A page of "X (2014) found, Y (2017) found" is an annotated bibliography wearing the clothes of a review

## What a Strong Review Does

- **It groups** sources by theme rather than by author or date
- **It names the convergence:** what these studies together have established
- **It adds nuance:** where they disagree, or where one qualifies another
- **It names a shared limitation**, which is usually where your gap lives
- Worked: survey research converges on livestream viewing being socially motivated, but all of it is self-report, so nobody has checked the behavioral trace

## The Same Thing, Written Out

> Livestream viewing is motivated less by what is on screen than by the social experience
> around it. Twitch streams function as virtual third places where informal communities
> form (Hamilton et al., 2014), and social and tension-release motivations are central to
> why viewers watch (Sjöblom & Hamari, 2017). Social interaction predicts not just
> watching but chatting and subscribing (Hilvert-Bruce et al., 2018). All three rely on
> self-report, leaving open whether the same patterns appear in behavioral chat-log data.

## What Self-Report Leaves Out

::: {.define}
**Self-report:** data in which people describe their own feelings, attitudes, or behavior, usually in a survey or an interview. Example: a viewer answering "I watch to feel part of a community" on a questionnaire.
:::

- **Behavioral trace data**, such as a chat log, records what people did rather than what they say they did

## Why That Version Works

- The **claim leads**, and the citations arrive behind it as support
- Sources are grouped by what they argue, not by the year they appeared
- The limitation is shared across the group, which makes it structural rather than a complaint about one paper
- The gap is never asserted. It falls out of the limitation on its own
- The paragraph points at a content analysis of a real chat log

## What to Mark in a Manuscript

- The **research question**, in the authors' own words, and the theory behind it
- The **design**: the unit of analysis, the sample, and how the key construct was measured
- The **finding** in one sentence, and the **gap** the authors claim to fill
- The **effect size** and the sample size used to detect it
- The **limitation the authors admit**, and the one they do not
- One sentence you would be willing to quote in your own methods section

## One Word From That List

::: {.define}
**Unit of analysis:** the one kind of thing each row of your coding sheet describes. Example: one chat message, or one TikTok video.
:::

- In someone else's article, find it by asking what one row of their data was

## The Number You Are Really There For

::: {.define}
**Effect size:** how big a difference or a relationship is, on a scale that does not grow with the sample. Example: how much longer non-gaming chat messages run than gaming ones.
:::

- It says how big the effect is, which is a different question from whether it cleared a significance threshold
- You need one because before you can justify how much data to collect, you need a defensible estimate of the effect you expect to find
- The most defensible source for that estimate is research that already measured it
- So you copy it out of their paper. That is the whole task

## What to Write Down

- Cohen's *d*, Cramer's *V*, or a correlation *r*, whichever the authors report, as defined on the next slide
- The *n* they used, because an effect size without a sample size is not much use
- Whether they ran a power analysis themselves, and what they assumed if so
- Those numbers become the inputs to your own **power analysis** later in the term
- A review that cannot supply an effect size estimate has not finished its job

## Three Effect Sizes You Will Meet

::: {.define}
**Cohen's *d*:** the difference between two group averages, measured in standard deviations, the usual spread of scores around an average. Example: a *d* of 0.5 means the two averages sit half a standard deviation apart.
:::

::: {.define}
**Cramer's *V*:** how strongly two categorical variables are associated, from 0 for none to 1 for complete. Example: whether channel type and viewer band tend to go together.
:::

::: {.define}
**Correlation (*r*):** how strongly two numeric variables rise or fall together in a straight-line pattern, from -1 to 1. Example: whether channels with more viewers also post more messages per minute.
:::

## Cohen on the Hard Part

> "Researchers find specifying the ES the most difficult part of power analysis."
>
> Cohen (1992, p. 156)

- ES is his abbreviation for effect size
- He is conceding that the hardest part is not the arithmetic
- The literature review is how that difficulty becomes tractable: you are not inventing an estimate, you are borrowing one from people who already did the measuring

## What That Looks Like When You Read

- Start with one study close to the kind of thing you want to do
- Find its primary effect size, and note whether the authors ran a power analysis themselves
- Later in the term you hand those numbers to the `pwr` package, which turns them into the sample size you need
- The harder case is coming: nobody has reported an effect for your question
- We will build **two** strategies for justifying a sample size anyway

## Discussion: A Power Primer {.discuss}

On Cohen (1992), "A power primer," answer each in writing:

- Cohen offers conventions for small, medium, and large effects. Conventions make a field legible. Name one thing they cost it
- He says specifying the effect size is the hardest part. Give one reason that step, and not the arithmetic, stalls people
- A paper this short has shaped decades of practice. Name one thing its brevity buys and one thing it leaves the reader to get wrong
- Name where you would expect to find an effect size for a question like yours, and say what you would do if nobody has reported one

## Four Kinds of Gap

- **Topical void:** a phenomenon, population, or context nobody has studied
- **Methodological gap:** a topic studied, but with methods carrying an important limitation
- **Contradiction:** two well-designed studies reaching opposite conclusions
- **Theoretical gap:** a phenomenon explained through one lens where another would show more

One caution on the void: what looks novel is usually covered under other terminology.

## Articulating the Gap

1. **Establish what is known.** Show you understand the conversation
2. **Identify the limitation.** Say what is missing, contradictory, or unexplained
3. **Argue for your study.** Say how your design addresses exactly that

The order is known, then limitation, then what this study does. The topic changes, and the
hinge does not.

## The Literature Map

- A markdown file in your project, organized by **theme** rather than alphabetically
- One heading per theme, sources beneath it, plus a running section for gaps
- It shows at a glance which themes are well covered and which are thin
- It makes you decide how sources relate, which is where synthesis starts
- Its structure usually becomes the structure of the written review
- Start it this week with the first article you read. Three headings and one source under one of them is already a map

## If That Feels Out of Reach

Start here. This is a floor, not a compromise:

- Source A, one sentence: what did this study find?
- Source B, one sentence: what did this study find?
- Source C, one sentence: what did this study find?
- The gap, one sentence: what do these three together leave unexplored?

Four sentences, three citations, and one gap are enough to anchor a Research Proposal. The
full synthesis paragraph is what it grows into, not where you start.

## Citation Is Ethical, Not Clerical

- Cite specific empirical findings, theoretical concepts, and methodological approaches
- Cite direct quotes always, and paraphrased ideas unless they are genuinely common knowledge
- No citation is needed for "Twitch is a livestreaming platform," for your own interpretations, or for your own data and analysis
- Nobody is criticized for citing too much. Under-citation damages credibility
- In its serious forms under-citation is plagiarism, which is a breach of trust before it is a rule

## One Finding, Three Explanations

Chapter 4 ended on a finding: livestream viewing looks more socially motivated than content
motivated. Three research programs explain that differently:

- **Uses and gratifications** (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973): viewers are active agents meeting a social need a finished video cannot meet
- **Parasocial interaction** (Horton & Wohl, 1956): viewers form one-sided bonds, and the social feeling is that bond being felt
- **Social identity** (Tajfel & Turner, 1979): the community is a group, and chat is a space of belonging

## Theory Is Not Speculation

::: {.define}
**Theory:** a set of connected ideas that explains and predicts why something happens, within stated limits. Example: parasocial interaction explains why viewers talk to a streamer as if they knew them.
:::

- A good theory is logically coherent, generalizable, falsifiable, and generative

## A Theory Makes Predictions

- Social identity theory predicts that viewers rate their own community above rivals on subjective dimensions like authenticity, and that they respond defensively when the streamer or community is criticized
- Change the domain and it predicts partisans rating aligned outlets as more credible
- The theory does not change. The domain does, and that is what makes it testable

## The Lens Metaphor

- A theory brings some things into focus and pushes others out of the frame
- **Appraisal theory** points at individual cognitive evaluation, so you build surveys and experiments measuring individual reaction
- **Social identity theory** points at group meaning, so you analyze how members talk about the stream and how boundaries get policed
- The same phenomenon gets different designs, and neither one is wrong
- You cannot use every lens at once. That produces blur rather than richness

## Three Paradigms

- **Social scientific:** an objective reality is observable and measurable
    - The work is deductive. It asks "does X cause Y?"
- **Interpretive:** reality is socially constructed through interaction
    - The work is inductive. It asks "what does X mean to the people who experience it?"
- **Critical and cultural:** power shapes what counts as knowledge
    - It asks "whose interests does X serve, and whose voices are silenced?"
- Each treats theory differently: as a source of predictions, as an outcome of observation, or as a tool for exposing structure

## Grand and Middle-Range Theories

- **Grand theories** explain human behavior across all contexts: Marxism, psychoanalysis, and structuralism
    - They are intellectually powerful, and too broad to design a study that could disprove them

::: {.define}
**Middle-range theory:** a theory specific enough to produce hypotheses you can test and general enough to apply beyond a single case. Example: social identity theory, which predicts how fans treat a rival community.
:::

- Merton named the zone, most communication research lives in it, and every theory in the catalogue ahead is middle-range

## The Catalogue: Relationships and Groups

[Horton & Wohl, 1956; Tajfel & Turner, 1979]{.eyebrow}

::: {.define}
**Parasocial interaction:** an audience member's one-sided sense of a social relationship with a media figure, experienced as if it ran both ways. Example: donating to a streamer you have never met.
:::

::: {.define}
**Social identity:** the part of a person's sense of self that comes from belonging to a group, which leads people to favor their own group over others. Example: regulars policing who belongs through the channel's own emotes and slang.
:::

## The Catalogue: Agendas and Frames

[McCombs & Shaw, 1972; Goffman, 1974; Entman, 1993]{.eyebrow}

::: {.define}
**Agenda setting:** the theory that media do not tell people what to think, but do shape what they think about, by choosing which issues get attention. Example: Twitch's front page and category rankings.
:::

::: {.define}
**Framing:** selecting some aspects of an issue and making them more prominent, which steers how an audience interprets and judges it. Example: how streamers title their own broadcasts.
:::

## The Catalogue: Audiences and Exposure

[Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973; Gerbner & Gross, 1976]{.eyebrow}

::: {.define}
**Uses and gratifications:** a theory that audiences actively choose media to meet their own needs, such as information, relaxation, or social connection. Example: a viewer who opens Twitch to feel part of a crowd.
:::

::: {.define}
**Cultivation:** the theory that heavy, long-term exposure to media gradually shapes people's beliefs about the real world toward what the media show. Example: a heavy viewer of crime shows who overestimates how common crime is.
:::

- Uses and gratifications is the lens behind most viewer-motivation research, and cultivation is strongest where audiences lack direct experience to check against

## Two Lenses, Four Messages

Here are four messages from one stretch of a real broadcast. Read them once before we code
them:

> **DragoBoi89:** xQc actually playing well today wtf
>
> **emotelord:** PogU PogU
>
> **realnamedfan:** @xqcow do u remember when u said hi to me last week
>
> **streamfan22:** chat is this real

## What Each Lens Foregrounds

- **Uses and gratifications** asks what need each viewer is meeting: evaluative commentary, collective emotional expression, direct acknowledgment, and group sense-making
    - All four viewers are equally interesting, because each one shows a different gratification
- **Parasocial interaction** asks what the bond looks like
    - realnamedfan's @-address plus a memory claim is the textbook case
    - emotelord and streamfan22 never address the streamer, so this lens pushes them aside
- The same data tells two stories, and your Research Proposal commits to one of them

## Choosing What to Read

- Start from the **keystone articles**: the ones your other sources keep citing
- Prefer studies close to your **design**, not only your topic. A content analysis of chat is worth more to you than a survey about streaming
- Take one that disagrees with the others if you can find it, because contradiction is a gap
- Fit beats recency. A 2016 study measuring what you want to measure beats a 2024 one that does not
- Three is the floor, not the target
